generation.hypothesis: Introduction of oxygen vacancies through high-temperature annealing can improve the resistance to thermally induced toughness loss in high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy in its as-cast or wrought state
generation.intervention: High-temperature annealing to introduce oxygen vacancies
generation.conditions: High-temperature annealing at temperatures above 800°C for several hours
generation.structural_mediator: Oxygen vacancies and their effects on the alloy's microstructure and mechanical properties
generation.mechanism: Derived from materials-science principles, as oxygen vacancies can alter the alloy's dislocation dynamics and grain boundary properties, leading to improved toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved resistance to thermally induced toughness loss, as measured by toughness tests such as Charpy impact testing
generation.boundary: Temperature range of 400°C to 800°C, where the alloy's toughness is known to decrease
generation.uncertainty: The exact temperature and time conditions for introducing oxygen vacancies, as well as the optimal level of oxygen vacancies for improved toughness

falsification_experiment.design: Charpy impact testing of high-entropy alloys with and without oxygen vacancies, introduced through high-temperature annealing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the toughness values of the alloy with oxygen vacancies are not significantly higher than those of the alloy without oxygen vacancies, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, we delved into the enhanced ductility and strength of the FeCoCrNiMo5−xCx-based medium-entropy alloy at cryogenic temperatures. Moreover, we conducted an in-depth analysis of the impact of carbides on the properties of the alloy. For the Mo5 and Mo4C1 alloys, yield strength and tensile strength showed a notable improvement when the temperatures were reduced to 77 K and 4.2 K. This improvement can be associated with the increased critical shear stress for plastic deformation and the resistance from the dislocation interactions under cryogenic conditions. It is clearly shown that the yield strength at cryogenic temperatures significantly surpasses the yield strength at ambient temperature. The results reveal that at reduced temperatures, deformation-induced twinning and martensitic transformation mechanisms are activated, significantly enhancing the work-hardening effects observable in the tensile engineering stress–strain curves. The dynamic Hall–Petch effect, which is attributable to twinning during deformation, is believed to be the underlying reason for the observed strain-hardening mechanics in the alloy.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs), which were originally developed as concentrated solid solutions of multiple principal elements in equal, or near equal, atomic ratios, have drawn progressively increasing attention over the past decade. Unlike single principal-element alloys, their complex alloy compositions and elemental distribution, together with crystal lattice distortion induced by atomic-size mismatch (depending upon relative atomic sizes), can have a significant effect on the activity of their crystal defects and hence mechanical properties. Although HEAs were initially designed to benefit from single-phase stabilization,, single-phase HEAs are actually not that common, and of those that do exist, only a few display excellent damage-tolerance in the form of combinations of high strength, ductility, and toughness. The well-studied equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi Cantor alloy and its derivatives, in particular the CrCoNi alloy, show exceptional damage-tolerance which progressively improves at cryogenic temperatures, although even these alloys do not have yield (as opposed to ultimate tensile) strengths that are comparable to some advanced steels.
